exam_mental.EMD1 2018-2019 Q2: n = 2 is −13.6/4 = −3.4 eV and the ionized state is 0, so it needs 3.4 eV.
exam_mental.EMD1 2018-2019 Q3: ΔE = 3.4 eV. Shortcut: hc/e = (6.62×10⁻³⁴ × 3×10⁸)/(1.6×10⁻¹⁹) ≈ 1240 eV·nm, so λ ≈ 1240/3.4 ≈ 365 nm. Only 367.8 nm is near it.
exam_mental.EMD1 2018-2019 Q4: ΔE = 10.2 eV, so λ ≈ 1240/10.2 ≈ 122 nm (1240/10 = 124, then a little less). Take the closest option, 122.6 nm.
exam_mental.EMD1 2019-2020 Q1: ΔE = −3.03 − (−5.14) = 2.11 eV. λ ≈ 1240/2.11 ≈ 590 nm = 5.9×10⁻⁷ m. A photon in the 10⁻²⁶ m range is absurd, so D goes first.
exam_mental.EMD1 2020-2021 Q5: Per atom: 2370×10³ / 6×10²³ ≈ 4×10⁻¹⁸ J. λ = hc/E ≈ 2×10⁻²⁵ / 4×10⁻¹⁸ = 5×10⁻⁸ m; with the exact 6.02 the value rounds to 5.04×10⁻⁸.
exam_mental.EMD1 2024-2025 Q5: 12.1 eV lifts the electron from −13.6 to −1.5 eV at most, which is n = 3. n = 2 (10.2 eV) and n = 3 (12.09 eV) are reachable; n = 4 (12.75 eV) is not.
exam_mental.EMD1 2025-2026 Q6: Count the pairs among levels 4, 3, 2, 1: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 lines.

questions.stem: About the physical quantities that characterize a wave:
options: The wavelength is the distance between two successive peaks
The period is the number of cycles per unit of time
The frequency is the inverse of the period and is expressed in hertz
The wave number is the inverse of the frequency
questions.explanation: λ is the length of one cycle and ν = 1/T, in Hz. The period is a time (the time for one cycle), and the number of cycles per unit of time is the frequency. The wave number is the inverse of the wavelength, not of the frequency.

questions.stem: About an electromagnetic wave:
options: The electric field E and the magnetic field B are parallel to each other
E and B oscillate at the same frequency
Its propagation speed depends on the medium
Its speed in a vacuum is 3×10⁶ m/s
questions.explanation: E and B oscillate at the same frequency and are perpendicular, not parallel. The speed depends on the medium and equals 3×10⁸ m/s in a vacuum, not 3×10⁶.

questions.stem: A radiation has a wavelength λ = 500 nm in a vacuum (c = 3×10⁸ m/s). For this radiation:
questions.explanation: ν = c/λ = 3×10⁸ / 5×10⁻⁷ = 6×10¹⁴ Hz, T = 1/ν ≈ 1.7×10⁻¹⁵ s, and 1/λ = 2×10⁶ m⁻¹. The value 2×10⁻³ is correct only in nm⁻¹, so option C has the wrong unit.
questions.mental: Convert first: 500 nm = 5×10⁻⁷ m. Then 3×10⁸ / 5×10⁻⁷ = 0.6×10¹⁵ = 6×10¹⁴ Hz, and T = 1/(6×10¹⁴) ≈ 0.17×10⁻¹⁴ s. The wave number is 1/(5×10⁻⁷) = 0.2×10⁷ = 2×10⁶ m⁻¹.

questions.stem: Which ranking of these radiations is in order of increasing wavelength?
options: Infrared < visible < ultraviolet < X-rays < gamma rays
X-rays < gamma rays < ultraviolet < visible < infrared
Gamma rays < X-rays < ultraviolet < visible < infrared
Gamma rays < X-rays < visible < ultraviolet < infrared
questions.explanation: Gamma rays have the shortest wavelengths, and the sequence runs through X-rays, ultraviolet, visible and infrared. Option A is the same list reversed, so it ranks by decreasing wavelength.

questions.stem: About the visible part of the electromagnetic spectrum:
options: It covers wavelengths from about 390 nm to about 760 nm
It is a narrow portion located roughly in the middle of the spectrum
questions.explanation: The visible range is about 390–760 nm, a narrow portion of a mostly invisible spectrum. Violet borders the ultraviolet and red merges into the infrared, so B and C swap the two ends.

questions.stem: Compare a photon of violet light (λ = 400 nm) with a photon of red light (λ = 700 nm):
options: The violet photon carries more energy
The energy of a photon is proportional to its frequency
The energy of a photon is proportional to its wavelength
The red photon has the higher frequency
questions.explanation: E = hν = hc/λ, so energy is proportional to frequency and inversely proportional to wavelength. The shorter-wavelength violet photon therefore has both the higher frequency and the higher energy.

questions.stem: A photon has a wavelength λ = 620 nm. Its energy is: (h = 6.62×10⁻³⁴ J·s; c = 3×10⁸ m/s; 1 eV = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J)
questions.explanation: E = hc/λ = (6.62×10⁻³⁴ × 3×10⁸) / (6.2×10⁻⁷) = 3.2×10⁻¹⁹ J = 2.0 eV. Option C comes from leaving λ in nm instead of converting to metres.
questions.mental: hc ≈ 2×10⁻²⁵ J·m, so E ≈ 2×10⁻²⁵ / 6.2×10⁻⁷ ≈ 3.2×10⁻¹⁹ J. Divide by 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ to get 2 eV. The shortcut λ(nm) ≈ 1240/E(eV) gives the same: 1240/620 = 2.

questions.stem: An electron transition releases a photon of energy 3.10 eV. The wavelength of this photon and its spectral region are: (h = 6.62×10⁻³⁴ J·s; c = 3×10⁸ m/s; 1 eV = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J)
questions.explanation: λ = hc/E ≈ 1240/3.10 = 400 nm, which lies inside the visible range (about 390–760 nm), at the violet end. Infrared starts beyond about 760 nm.
questions.mental: λ(nm) ≈ 1240/E(eV), because hc/e = (6.62×10⁻³⁴ × 3×10⁸)/(1.6×10⁻¹⁹) ≈ 1240 eV·nm. So 1240/3.1 = 400 nm. Options B and D fail immediately: 40 nm is not visible and 4000 nm is not ultraviolet.

questions.stem: An electron (m = 9.1×10⁻³¹ kg) moves at v = 2.18×10⁶ m/s. The wavelength of the associated De Broglie wave is: (h = 6.62×10⁻³⁴ J·s)
questions.explanation: λ = h/mv = 6.62×10⁻³⁴ / (9.1×10⁻³¹ × 2.18×10⁶) ≈ 3.3×10⁻¹⁰ m = 3.3 Å. Option C is the ratio inverted (mv/h).

questions.stem: A particle of mass m = 6.62×10⁻²⁷ kg travels at v = 10³ m/s. Its De Broglie wavelength is: (h = 6.62×10⁻³⁴ J·s)
questions.mental: The 6.62 cancels, leaving only powers of ten: 10⁻³⁴ / 10⁻²⁴ = 10⁻¹⁰ m = 1 Å.

questions.stem: About De Broglie's relation:
options: A wave of wavelength λ = h/mv can be associated with any moving material particle
Doubling the speed of a particle doubles its wavelength
At the same speed, the heavier particle has the shorter wavelength
For an electron in orbit, the total length of the orbit is an integer multiple of its wavelength
questions.explanation: λ = h/mv makes the wavelength inversely proportional to both mass and speed, so doubling v halves λ. The standing-wave condition is 2πr = nλ.

questions.stem: In the De Broglie model, an electron of the hydrogen atom is on the orbit n = 2, of radius r = 2.12 Å. Its wavelength λ is:
questions.explanation: The standing-wave condition is 2πr = nλ, so λ = 2πr/n = 2π × 2.12 / 2 ≈ 6.66 Å. Option C forgets to divide by n = 2.
questions.mental: With n = 2 the 2 cancels, so λ = πr ≈ 3.14 × 2.12: 3 × 2.12 = 6.36, plus about 0.3, gives about 6.66 Å.

questions.stem: The figure shows the spectra obtained when two different light sources are passed through a glass prism (upper and lower panels). Which statements are correct?
options: The upper spectrum is continuous, as produced by light from an incandescent tungsten bulb
The lower spectrum is a line spectrum, as produced by an electrical discharge in low-pressure hydrogen
Sunlight dispersed by a prism would give a spectrum like the lower one
The prism separates the radiation into its characteristic wavelengths
questions.explanation: White light (sunlight, incandescent solids) gives a continuous spectrum, while a low-pressure gas discharge gives discrete lines. Sunlight would therefore look like the upper panel, not the lower one.

questions.stem: About Rutherford's planetary model of the atom:
options: The orbiting electron gains energy and moves away from the nucleus
According to electrodynamics, the orbiting electron should emit electromagnetic radiation
The electron should end up falling into the nucleus, which contradicts the existence of the atom
Bohr resolved this contradiction in 1913 with a model based on the quantization of energy
questions.explanation: The emitted radiation carries energy away, so the electron should lose energy and spiral inward, not gain energy and move away. Since atoms exist, this is a contradiction, which Bohr's model addressed.

questions.stem: About Bohr's postulates for the hydrogen atom:
options: First postulate: the electron moves on elliptical orbits whose energy varies
Second postulate: the angular momentum mvr is an integer multiple of h/2π
Third postulate: during a transition between two orbits, ΔE = |En₁ − En₂| = hν
Third postulate: the electron radiates continuously while it stays on an orbit
questions.explanation: The first postulate describes stationary circular orbits of constant energy. Radiation is absorbed or emitted only during a transition between orbits, with ΔE = hν.

questions.stem: Consider the levels n = 2 and n = 4 of the hydrogen atom. According to Bohr's model:
options: Going from n = 2 to n = 4, the electron absorbs radiation
Going from n = 4 to n = 2, the electron emits radiation
The radiation absorbed in 2→4 and the radiation emitted in 4→2 have the same wavelength
While it stays on n = 4, the electron continuously emits radiation
questions.explanation: Moving up absorbs and moving down emits, and both transitions have the same ΔE = |E₄ − E₂| = hν, so the same frequency and wavelength. On a stationary orbit the energy stays constant, so there is no emission.

questions.stem: The radius of the orbit n = 3 of the hydrogen atom is: (a₀ = 0.53 Å)
questions.explanation: rₙ = a₀n², so r₃ = 9 × 0.53 = 4.77 Å. Option A multiplies by n instead of n², and D is the radius of n = 2.

questions.stem: The electron of a hydrogen atom moves from n = 1 to n = 2. (a₀ = 0.53 Å; E₁ = −13.6 eV) In the new orbit:
options: The speed of the electron is divided by 2
The energy of the electron is −3.4 eV
questions.explanation: The radius grows as n² (rₙ = a₀n², ×4 here, giving 2.12 Å). The speed falls as 1/n (vₙ = v₀/n) and the energy goes as 1/n² (−13.6/4 = −3.4 eV).
questions.mental: Use the scaling with n = 2: radius × 4 (0.53 × 4 = 2.12 Å), speed ÷ 2, energy ÷ 4 (13.6/4 = 3.4 eV).

questions.stem: About the energy of the electron in a stationary orbit of radius r:
options: The total energy is the sum of the kinetic energy and the potential energy
The kinetic energy is Ec = Ke²/2r
The total energy equals the opposite of the kinetic energy
questions.explanation: Ep = −Ke²/r and Ec = Ke²/2r, so E_T = −Ke²/r + Ke²/2r = −Ke²/2r = −Ec. Option C gives the potential energy, not the total energy.

questions.stem: Combining the balance of forces with the quantization of angular momentum gives the radius of the Bohr orbit:
questions.explanation: The boxed result is r = n²h²/(4Kmₑπ²e²), which is a₀n²; for n = 1 it gives about 0.53 Å. Option A has n instead of n², and B is the fraction inverted.

questions.stem: The energy of the level n = 2 of the hydrogen atom is: (E₁ = −13.6 eV = −21.76×10⁻¹⁹ J)
questions.explanation: Eₙ = E₁/n², so E₂ = E₁/4 = −3.40 eV = −5.44×10⁻¹⁹ J. Options C and D divide by n instead of n².
questions.mental: Divide by n² = 4 by halving twice: 13.6 → 6.8 → 3.4, and 21.76 → 10.88 → 5.44. One halving only is the trap in C and D.

questions.stem: Using the energy diagram of the hydrogen atom in the figure (energies in eV), the smallest energy that an electron on level n = 2 must absorb to reach level n = 5 is:
questions.explanation: ΔE = E₅ − E₂ = −0.54 − (−3.40) = 2.86 eV. Option B adds the two magnitudes instead of taking the difference.
questions.mental: Take the difference of the magnitudes when both levels are negative: 3.40 − 0.54 = 2.86 eV.

questions.stem: A hydrogen atom in its ground state (E₁ = −13.6 eV; E₂ = −3.40 eV; E₃ = −1.51 eV; E₄ = −0.85 eV) receives photons of various energies. Which photons can it absorb?
questions.explanation: A photon is absorbed only if hν equals a gap between two levels: 10.2 eV reaches n = 2 and 12.75 eV reaches n = 4. A photon of 11.0 or 5.0 eV matches no gap, because energy is quantized.
questions.mental: Add each photon energy to −13.6 and see if a real level appears: 10.2 gives −3.40 (n = 2), 12.75 gives −0.85 (n = 4), 11.0 gives −2.6 and 5.0 gives −8.6, which are not levels.

questions.stem: The smallest energy needed to ionize a hydrogen atom whose electron is on level n = 3 is: (E₃ = −1.51 eV)
questions.explanation: The ionized state has E∞ = 0, so ΔE = 0 − (−1.51) = 1.51 eV. The value 13.6 eV applies from the ground state, and 12.09 eV is the gap from n = 1 to n = 3.

questions.stem: The electrons of a hydrogen sample are excited to level n = 5. Counting every possible return path to the ground state, how many different lines can the emission spectrum show?
questions.explanation: Each pair of levels among n = 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 gives one line: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10. The value 4 counts only single-step returns.
questions.mental: Add from the top: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10, which is n(n − 1)/2 with n = 5.

questions.stem: Which transitions of the hydrogen atom emit visible radiation (about 390–760 nm)? (E₁ = −13.6 eV; E₂ = −3.40 eV; E₃ = −1.51 eV; E₄ = −0.85 eV; h = 6.62×10⁻³⁴ J·s; c = 3×10⁸ m/s; 1 eV = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J)
questions.explanation: With λ = hc/ΔE: 3→2 (1.89 eV) gives about 657 nm and 4→2 (2.55 eV) gives about 487 nm, both visible. 2→1 (10.2 eV) gives about 122 nm, in the ultraviolet, and 4→3 (0.66 eV) gives about 1880 nm, in the infrared.
questions.mental: With λ(nm) ≈ 1240/E(eV), visible light means E from about 1240/760 ≈ 1.6 eV to 1240/390 ≈ 3.2 eV. Just check which gaps fall in that window: 1.89 and 2.55 do, 10.2 and 0.66 don't.

questions.stem: About the energy diagram of the hydrogen atom:
options: The ionized state corresponds to E∞ = 0
The first excited state is the level n = 1
The gaps between successive levels get smaller as n increases
The ground state has an energy of −13.6 eV, which is −21.76×10⁻¹⁹ J
questions.explanation: n = 1 is the ground state, and the excited states start at n = 2. The levels crowd together toward E∞ = 0: the gap is 10.2 eV for 1→2 but only 0.31 eV for 4→5.
